groups.text: Here is the FX rate cache from this lesson's lab.
On a miss, it does a one hundred ms socket read, while it holds the cache's monitor.
In Kotlin, the Synchronized annotation makes the same monitor.
The J D K runs virtual threads on carrier threads, one per core.
Say there are four.
VT one to four call rate.
VT five and six never touch the cache.
VT one mounts on carrier one, enters rate, and takes the monitor.
On J D K twenty-one to twenty-three, the J V M records a monitor's owner per O S thread.
So the owner is carrier one.
Now VT one starts the socket read.
A blocking read normally unmounts a virtual thread.
But while VT one holds the monitor, it can't leave its carrier.
It is pinned, and carrier one blocks with it.
VT two, three and four mount and call rate.
The monitor is taken, so each one blocks, and each one is pinned too.
All four carriers are stuck, and the C P U does nothing.
Four callers of rate have stopped every virtual thread in the J V M, even VT five and six, which never touch the cache.
Now use a ReentrantLock instead.
In Kotlin, withLock writes the try and finally for you.
Again, VT one to VT four mount and call rate.
VT one takes the lock first.
VT one starts the read.
ReentrantLock parks the thread the normal way, so VT one unmounts to the heap, and it still holds the lock.
VT two, three and four ask for the lock.
Each one parks and unmounts too.
Now the carriers are free, and they run VT five and six.
When the rate arrives, VT one mounts again on a free carrier, stores the rate and unlocks.
Then VT two gets the lock, and mounts on the last free carrier.
J D K twenty-four fixed this with JEP four hundred ninety-one.
A virtual thread can now take, hold and release a monitor independently of its carrier, so synchronized and Object.wait unmount like ReentrantLock.
J D K twenty-five is the first LTS release with the fix.
So on J D K twenty-five, leave working synchronized code alone.
On J D K twenty-one, put a ReentrantLock around blocking calls.
